title: Darkening a photo is not the same as driving at night
paper_title: Questioning Post-hoc Image Corruptions as a Proxy for Environmental Variation in Autonomous Driving
date_note: Information Society 2026 multiconference, Ljubljana, early October 2026 (proceedings Vol. 1, pp. 60-63); exact day approximate
summary: A short guide to the post-hoc corruptions paper: a darkening filter and a simulated night look alike but test a driving agent very differently. Full write-up on the LANCER page.
cta: Read the full write-up on the LANCER page

body.p: This paper belongs to LANCER, my postdoctoral project at the University of Ljubljana on autonomous navigation in complex environments using reinforcement learning. Part of that work is testing: how do we know a camera-driven car will cope with night or fog?

The common shortcut is to take recorded footage and damage it with image filters, such as darkening it or adding a fog-like veil, then see how badly the vision network copes. It hides an assumption: that the filtered picture stands in for the physical condition it is named after. We tested it in a driving simulator that can produce night and fog in two ways. One filters the finished picture. The other changes the lights and the fog in the scene before it is rendered. We matched each filter to its physical condition by how much it changes the picture, and let nine independently trained agents drive in both.

figure.alt: Two rows of frames: with simulated night the car leaves the road, while with the matched darkening filter it completes the run; for fog the physical condition and its filter look and behave alike.
figure.caption: The same road, agent and random seed, driven by the most fragile of the nine agents, chosen because the failure is easy to see. The simulated night puts the car off the road. The filter that matches it does not.

body.p: Fog passed the test: the real fog and its filter agree at every strength. Night did not. At a picture change of 38 grey levels, the physical night cost the nine agents 0.51 of their driving performance, while the matched darkening filter cost nothing measurable. All nine agents agreed (sign test, p = 0.004). Training with filters did not help either: against physical conditions an agent trained that way did slightly worse (8.68 laps out of ten, against 9.05 without), while an agent that also saw re-rendered conditions completed every lap.

So whether a filter is a fair stand-in depends on the physics of the condition it imitates. These are simulator measurements, and our night has no headlights, which plausibly overstates what darkness does to a lit vehicle. The details, including a distance-based test we tried, are on the project page.
